abandon: The only evidence for the mechanism is that the base's 'Answer:' answers are more accurate overall: result-fdc8da, "'Answer:' line median -8.36 (n=132, 121 right)", against roughly 289 of 338 boxed answers right. The same item splits the base's quick wrong answers by marker, and that split goes the other way. It reports "wrong answers under 4,000 tokens median -0.53 (n=21)" and says "RL gives a wrong box the base's probability (median D 0.001, n=10)". Only about 10 of the roughly 49 wrong boxed answers are boxed answers under 4,000 tokens. That leaves about 11 quick wrong answers that are not boxed. Only about 30 finished rows carry neither marker, so at least 8 of those 11 must be 'Answer:' answers. In other words, most of the 11 wrong 'Answer:' answers are quick ones. 'Answer:' answers are at most 132 of the roughly 350 quick answers (about 0.38; result-5e17a6 counts "Base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, 13 wrong."). Yet they make up about half of the 21 quick wrong answers. So among quick answers, 'Answer:' answers are wrong at least as often as boxed ones (about 9 % vs about 4 %). The boxed answers' extra errors are almost all long answers on hard problems. So the overall 'Answer:' advantage comes from which problems each marker lands on (difficulty and length), not from a less accurate boxed register at matched difficulty. A further point against reading the marker as a register: knowledge-8229be finds that boxing goes together with higher accuracy, not lower. In every arm that recovers accuracy, "Every arm that recovers accuracy also takes RL's format and length: 'Answer:' line in 0-4 % of answers vs 39-46 % for base-like arms". RL itself boxes in 100 % of answers (knowledge-499152: "'Answer:' line share base 0.44, RL 0.00"). So a large boxed share cannot be part of the cue-to-RL gap. The mechanism's first test (a within-quartile difference of at least +5 points) is therefore expected to fail, and building predictions on it would waste the tests.
